vignette:
The first time he tells it—sitting in the chair across from me, his hands clasped tight over his knees—he keeps his eyes on the floor. He says he doesn’t remember the sound of the gunshot, only the way the air changed. One moment he was walking out of the supply store, a box of hair relaxer tucked under his arm, a new pair of clippers in a plastic bag swinging from his wrist. The next, there was a man in front of him, a dark hood, a voice that said *give it up, old man*. He gave it up. Wallet, bag, the box of relaxer. But the man wanted more. He wanted everything. He wanted the watch his father had given him, and when he hesitated—just a second, just a breath—the butt of the pistol came down across his temple.

That was six months ago.

Now he works the same shop, the one he’s owned for twenty years on the busy street in Accra. The mirrors are still there, the black leather chairs, the smell of perm and shea butter. But something has changed. He no longer likes to stand with his back to the door. He positions his station so he can see the entrance at all times. When a customer comes in too quickly, his scissors pause mid-snip. When a delivery boy knocks, he flinches. He wants to laugh about it, to call himself foolish, but the laugh gets stuck.

He is a good hairdresser—patient, steady, someone who listens while his hands work. Before, he could cut for hours, chatting about football, politics, the price of eggs. Now he finds himself losing the thread mid-sentence. A client will ask a question, and he will hear the words but not the meaning. His mind is somewhere else. Sometimes it is back in that alley. He feels the cold of the concrete through his knees, hears his own voice begging in a language he barely uses anymore. He has to blink hard, shake his head, and ask the client to repeat themselves. They think he is getting old. Maybe he is.

At night, his wife tells him he talks in his sleep. Not words—sounds. Grunts. A cry that wakes her. Sometimes he wakes himself, sitting bolt upright, heart hammering, convinced the hooded man is in the room. He checks the locks three times before bed. Once, twice, a third time with a breath that rattles. His wife asks what is wrong, and he says nothing, because what is there to say? That he feels like a stranger in his own life? That the street he has walked for decades now feels like a trap? That he no longer goes to the supply store unless his son drives him, and even then he sits in the car, heart racing, while his son runs inside?

He has not told anyone the full story. Not his wife. Not his brother. He tells himself it was just money, just a watch, just a bump on the head. He should be fine. But the world feels thin now. A loud noise—a car backfiring, a door slamming—sends a jolt through him. He avoids the market, avoids crowds, avoids the alley by the pharmacy. His hands, steady for so many years, tremble when he holds a comb. He blames it on age, on fatigue. But it is not age.

And yet, he still shows up. Every morning, he unlocks the shop, turns on the radio, wipes down the mirrors. The customers come. He smiles, greets them, asks about their families. He picks up his scissors. And for a few moments, the work takes over—the rhythm of the cut, the glide of the clippers, the familiar weight of trust in his hands. But then a car honks outside. A voice rises in laughter. And he is back in that alley, his temple wet, his father’s watch gone forever.
